newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA PLANNED WEAPON SALE TO YUGOSLAVIA - DE KOCK.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA PLANNED WEAPON SALE TO YUGOSLAVIA - DE KOCK.

text.p: Plans to sell South Africa's prize weapons of war to Yugoslavia in the early 1990s were scuttled when the United States became suspicious of Pretoria, an apartheid-era assassin revealed on Wednesday.

Ex-police colonel Eugene de Kock told a court where he is pleading for leniency after his conviction for six murders that negotiations on the sale of the long-range G5 and G6 cannons were under way when the U.S. interest torpedoed the deal.
"The process was going well until America got a sniff of it under its nose," said de Kock, the former commander of a secret death-squad unit run by the regime to hunt black guerrillas.

He did not disclose if the weapons deal was negotiated before or after war broke out between the former Yugoslavian republics, in 1991, nor whether it was with the old Yugoslavian government or breakaway republics.
The South African government had revised arms sales to the area when it became unstable, and in 1993 declared there could be "no trade whatsoever" with rump Yugoslavia.
De Kock said he and three others would each have received $1.2 million if the weapons deal had gone through.
"I would act as a facilitator between parties... My commission would have been 20 percent," he added.
He testified he had first visited Yugoslavia to attend a major weapons exhibition in Serbia in 1989, when the eastern European country was already becoming volatile.
Thereafter, he said, he had travelled numerous times to the republics of Slovenia, Croatia and Serbia.

De Kock, a 47-year-old career policeman, is testifying in the hope of escaping a life sentence. He has begun naming his superiors in the highest ranks in order to prove the crimes he committed were done according to orders.
